reference.source: Occupational and Environmental Respiratory Medicine reference texts
clinicalPearls: Results from inhalation of iron oxide fume or dust, classically in electric-arc welders, oxy-acetylene cutters, and foundry workers
Pure siderosis is generally a benign, non-fibrotic deposition disease with little or no functional impairment
Radiographs may show widespread fine nodular or reticular opacities that can be striking despite few symptoms
Imaging changes may partially regress after exposure ceases, reflecting clearance of iron-laden macrophages
Iron oxide deposits accumulate as macrophage-laden macules around small airways and vessels without significant collagen deposition
Mixed exposures, especially to silica (siderosilicosis), can convert a benign picture into a fibrotic one
A clear welding or metalworking history is essential, as the radiographic burden may otherwise prompt unnecessary invasive workup
reference.pathophysiology: Fine iron oxide particles generated during welding and metal cutting are inhaled and deposited in the lung, where alveolar macrophages engulf them and accumulate as pigmented aggregates around respiratory bronchioles and perivascular spaces. Because iron oxide is relatively inert and provokes minimal fibrogenic response, pure siderosis produces macule deposition without meaningful interstitial fibrosis, and the process is largely benign and potentially partly reversible. When welding fume also contains silica or other fibrogenic dusts, a mixed pneumoconiosis with genuine fibrosis (siderosilicosis) can develop, and welders additionally face increased risks of airways disease and metal fume fever.
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph and high-resolution CT to characterise nodular or reticular opacities
Detailed welding and metalworking occupational history
Spirometry and diffusing capacity to confirm preserved function in pure disease
Bronchoalveolar lavage showing iron-laden macrophages where sampling is undertaken
Serial imaging to observe partial regression after exposure ends
redFlags: Progressive breathlessness or fibrosis suggesting mixed-dust disease rather than pure siderosis
New mass or cavitation raising concern for malignancy or tuberculosis
Significant functional decline inconsistent with benign iron deposition
Systemic symptoms prompting search for an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Pure siderosis is benign, usually asymptomatic, and may partially clear after exposure ceases; prognosis worsens only when there is concurrent silica exposure producing fibrosis or coexisting airways disease.
pitfalls: Assuming impressive radiographic nodularity implies severe functional disease
Failing to identify coexisting silica exposure that changes prognosis
Proceeding to invasive biopsy when a clear welding history and benign course suffice
Overlooking welding-related airflow obstruction or metal fume fever as separate entities
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Removal from further iron oxide fume and dust exposure, with workplace controls such as local exhaust ventilation and respiratory protection
Reassurance that pure siderosis is benign and imaging may partly regress after exposure ceases, so no specific drug therapy is required
Smoking cessation support to limit additional airways disease
Serial chest imaging and spirometry with diffusing capacity to confirm preserved function and detect any evolving fibrosis
Assessment for coexisting silica exposure that could cause a fibrotic siderosilicosis
Occupational health referral and reporting as an occupational lung disease
